newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO in U.S.-sponsored security talks.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO in U.S.-sponsored security talks.

text.p: Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. security officials held talks on Sunday in the Ramallah West Bank Palestinian enclave as part of a framework set by U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, Israel security sources said.

The sources said they hoped to receive data from the Palestinians on explosives found in early July by the Palestinians at a West Bank apartment they suspected was a bomb laboratory of the anti-Israeli Hamas movement.
A leaflet in Hamas's name claimed responsibility for a July 30 double bombing of a Jerusalem market. Israeli and Palestinian officials have questioned the authenticity of the claim.
The attackers, who died along with 14 other people at the market frequented by Israelis, have yet to be identified.
The bombing deepened a peacemaking crisis that followed Israel's launching of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the Palestinian Authority of not doing enough to fight guerrillas in its territory who opposed the peace process.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has said Netanyahu is using the bombing to destroy the peace process he inherited from Israel's Labour government ousted in May 1996 elections.
Ross spent four days in the region last week, arranging Israel-PLO security talks attended by U.S. representatives after the bombing.

He was also preparing the ground for a visit to the Middle East planned for September by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. She has demanded improved Israeli-Palestinian security cooperation before she makes her maiden trip to the region.

Britain's Sunday Telegraph newspaper said on Sunday that Israel's Shin Bet secret police chief Ami Ayalon was in London to investigate claims the bombing was carried out by Arab guerrillas based in Britain.
A spokesman for Netanyahu's office was checking the report.
The militant Hamas and Islamic Jihad movements have waged violent opposition to Israel-PLO interim peace deals, killing scores of Israelis.

Israeli government sources said that on Sunday, in a sign of a slight easing of tensions between the sides, Netanyahu sent an envoy to thank Arafat for aid in finding the Palestinian killers of an Israeli taxi driver at the weekend. The men were car thieves.
They said the envoy, Yitzhak Molho, secretly met the Palestinian president in Gaza on Saturday night.
The sources said the men also discussed Ross's visit and sanctions Israel imposed on Palestinians after the bombing.
There was no immediate indication of any easing of the sanctions following Saturday's meeting.

Israel demanded Arafat arrest militants and crush the infrastructure of Islamist groups after the suicide attacks. It also sealed off Palestinian areas and froze millions of dollars of financial transfers it owes the Palestinian Authority (PA).
The Palestinians say the measures are collective punishment.
Washington has also repeatedly condemned Israel's sanctions as "counterproductive" and "unhelpful". The PA has said it will match the sanctions with a partial boycott on Israeli goods.
Arafat rejected on Sunday Israeli allegations that his planned "national unity" talks with militant groups set for this week amounted to "appeasement of terrorism".
"No doubt we are against terrorist activities...but this is a Palestinian interest and we are insisting to carry on dialogue with all Palestinian groups," Arafat told reporters in Gaza.
"We are as Palestinians completely committed to the peace process and at the same time we are facing collective punishment from the Israeli government," Arafat said.
Hamas took part in a first round of unity talks in February. It boycotted a round in April, saying Arafat jailed Hamas men.
The Palestinian Authority says it is making "100 percent effort" on security but refuses to take orders from Israel.
Netanyahu insists he will ease the sanctions hand-in-hand with Palestinian measures against militants.
